intro: Rimsky-Korsakov’s 1886 concert version of Night on Bald Mountain depicts a witches’ sabbath that ends at the sound of a village church bell. Racing violins and threatening brass are followed by a long dawn.

sections.label: A · Allegro feroce, violins and brass
sections.mNote: The Allegro feroce opens with the two violin sections alone.

sections.label: B · Short dances for wind and strings
sections.mNote: Detached figures pass between woodwinds and strings.

sections.label: C · Long phrases over muted violins
sections.mNote: The woodwinds hold their tune above repeated string figures.

sections.label: A′ · Brass theme returns
sections.mNote: Quick string figures alternate with the opening’s heavy brass phrases.

sections.label: D · Bell in D over strings
sections.mNote: A bell in D sounds above quiet strings.

sections.label: Coda · Clarinet and flute at daybreak
sections.mNote: Solo woodwinds play above low strings and harp.

relations.label: The opening agitation returns
relations.basis: In Rimsky-Korsakov’s concert version, opening fast material returns after contrasting episodes; these excerpts link the opening with the renewed-pressure section marked near 365 s. CENS diagonal mean 0.924, sustained 15.5 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 343.5 s (cache/form/mussorgsky-night-bald-mountain.txt, candidate 3; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Opening, violins alone
cues.text: The two violin sections begin alone, pianissimo, with quick interlocking figures. The marking is Allegro feroce, fast and ferocious. Low strings soon enter with a pulse beneath them, and flute and oboe play their first held notes.
cues.evidence: Rimsky-Korsakov’s concert score, Bessel edition, p. 3, first four bars: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/4/48/IMSLP139196-PMLP04739-Mussorgsky_-_Night_on_Bald_Mountain_FS_rsl.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Borodin meets Mussorgsky, 1856
cues.text: In autumn 1856 Borodin, an army doctor on duty at a Saint Petersburg military hospital, met the seventeen-year-old Guards officer Mussorgsky. That evening Mussorgsky, in a close-fitting uniform, with pomaded hair and immaculate nails, played extracts from Il trovatore and La traviata. In 1858 he petitioned to leave the army.
cues.evidence: Borodin’s own account of the meeting, in the hospital duty room and that evening at the chief physician’s house, is quoted in Georgy Khubov’s biography of Mussorgsky, ch. 3 (Russian; translation ours): http://mussorgsky.ru/hubov019.html . The petition to leave the regiment is dated 1 May 1858 in Istoriya russkoy muzyki, vol. 7, Mussorgsky chapter: https://lib.rmvoz.ru/bigzal/irm/7/musorgskij/st

cues.title: Printed programme, 1886
cues.text: The printed programme describes underground voices, spirits of darkness and Chernobog, the Black God. His followers celebrate a black mass and a sabbath. The sound of a distant village church bell breaks up the gathering, and day returns.
cues.evidence: Bessel score, p. 2, Russian and French programme printed with Rimsky-Korsakov’s 1886 preface.

cues.title: Letter to Vladimir Nikolsky, 1867
cues.text: In July 1867, weeks after finishing the score, Mussorgsky told the literary scholar Vladimir Nikolsky that he saw in this “sinful prank” an original Russian work, nourished on Russian bread. Balakirev rejected it and would not have it performed. Mussorgsky later returned to the music and recast it for the stage.
cues.evidence: Mussorgsky to V. V. Nikolsky, Minkino, 12 July 1867 (“sinful prank”, “nourished on Russian bread”: our translation of the Russian), quoted in Istoriya russkoy muzyki, vol. 7, note 73: https://lib.rmvoz.ru/bigzal/irm/7/musorgskij/st . Balakirev’s refusal to perform the piece at the Free Music School: https://www.belcanto.ru/mussorgsky_night.html . Rimsky-Korsakov, My Musical Life, p. 220, on Balakirev’s criticism and the versions for Mlada and The Fair at Sorochyntsy: https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/72/IMSLP721391-PMLP52433-My_Musical_Life_eng_edt.pdf

cues.title: Concert version, Saint Petersburg, 1886
cues.text: Five years after Mussorgsky’s death, Rimsky-Korsakov assembled this concert piece from his friend’s manuscripts. Much of it came through the later choral version for The Fair at Sorochyntsi.
cues.evidence: Rimsky-Korsakov dates his preface Saint Petersburg, 1886, in the Bessel score, p. 2. The Sorochyntsi source and recomposition are discussed at https://www.laphil.com/works/night-on-bald-mountain

cues.title: Bell in D, rehearsal W
cues.text: A bell tuned to D sounds as the dance breaks up. The tempo slows to Poco meno mosso, with a quiet violin tremolo and the cellos playing D pizzicato. The trombones, tuba, bass drum and cymbals, which carried the sabbath, stop.
cues.evidence: Bessel score, p. 60, rehearsal W: Campana in D, Poco meno mosso, quiet violin tremolo and pizzicato cellos on D; trombones, tuba, bass drum and cymbals cease.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Bell and tam-tam, première, 1886
cues.text: In Mussorgsky’s last version, for his opera The Fair at Sorochyntsi, the sabbath is a sleeping peasant lad’s dream, and a village bell ends it. At the 1886 première the bell chosen at the bell-store went off pitch in the hall as the temperature changed. A tam-tam was used in its place.
cues.evidence: Rimsky-Korsakov, My Musical Life (Joffe translation), p. 221: in the version for The Fair at Sorochyntsy the peasant lad sees the witches’ sabbath in a dream and the piece ends with the ringing of the village church bell. P. 236, on the first Russian Symphony Concert of the 1886–87 season: “Only a tamtam had to be substituted for the bell”, the one he chose at the bell-store being off pitch in the hall “owing to a change in temperature”. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/7/72/IMSLP721391-PMLP52433-My_Musical_Life_eng_edt.pdf

cues.title: Clarinet solo, Meno mosso
cues.text: Meno mosso, tranquillo. A solo clarinet plays dolce, sweetly, above divided violas and low strings, and the violins rest. D is held in the bass under the clarinet’s turns.
cues.evidence: Bessel score, p. 64, rehearsal Y: Meno mosso, Tranquillo, solo clarinet marked dolce, divided violas, cellos and double basses.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Solo flute, rehearsal Z
cues.text: A solo flute takes the next phrase, also marked dolce. The double basses play their low notes pizzicato while divided violas and bowed cellos sustain the harmony. The flute’s last notes are marked perdendosi.
cues.evidence: Bessel score, p. 64, rehearsal Z: solo flute marked dolce and perdendosi, divided violas, bowed cellos and pizzicato double basses.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Repin’s portrait, hospital, 1881
cues.text: In March 1881 Ilya Repin painted Mussorgsky in the Nikolaevsky Military Hospital in Saint Petersburg over four sittings. The sitter wore a hospital robe with crimson lapels. Mussorgsky died there on 28 March, a week after his forty-second birthday.
cues.evidence: The Tretyakov Gallery, which owns the portrait, says Repin came to the Nikolaevsky Military Hospital on four days, 2–5 March (Old Style), and painted Mussorgsky in a hospital robe, red at the lapels and green in the folds; Mussorgsky died on 16 March (Old Style), 28 March in the modern calendar: https://my.tretyakov.ru/app/masterpiece/20705 (Russian). He was born on 9 (21) March 1839, and Khubov places his death in the same hospital: http://mussorgsky.ru/hubov001.html and http://mussorgsky.ru/hubov009.html (Russian).

cues.title: Close in D major
cues.text: Harp arpeggios and quiet wind chords bring the music to rest in D major. The strings return for the last soft chord, and the basses play a final pizzicato D. The score ends with a fermata over a rest.
cues.evidence: Bessel score, p. 65: harp arpeggios, final D major harmony, pizzicato low strings and final rest with fermata.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: The bell holds D as the dance stops
transitions.to: D · Bell in D over strings
transitions.how: The rushing strings descend and diminish. At Poco meno mosso (rehearsal W), a bell tuned to D begins its slow tolling. The cellos pluck D beneath quiet violin tremolo. The clarinets hold their chord and the flutes move in longer notes. The trombones, tuba, bass drum and cymbals stop playing at this point.
transitions.evidence: Bessel score, p. 60, rehearsal W: descending strings, Campana in D, Poco meno mosso and the marked cessation of the heavy brass and percussion.

transitions.title: Clarinet solo over low D
transitions.from: D · Bell in D over strings
transitions.to: Coda · Clarinet and flute at daybreak
transitions.how: The moving violin figures stop. At Meno mosso, tranquillo, a solo clarinet plays over divided violas, cellos and double basses, with D held low. Harp arpeggios follow the end of its phrase, and a solo flute then takes up the dawn music.
transitions.evidence: Bessel score, pp. 63–64, rehearsals Y–Z: the violin parts cease, clarinet and flute solos alternate over low D, and harp arpeggios connect the phrases.

source.title: Mussorgsky, Night on Bald Mountain, Rimsky-Korsakov’s concert version, full score (Bessel)
source.locator: Opening, p. 3; woodwind and string dances, pp. 14–36; bell and dispersal at W, p. 60; clarinet and flute solos at Y–Z, p. 64; D major close, p. 65.

timeline.note: The two violin sections begin alone, pianissimo, in running figures.
Short woodwind and string phrases alternate with brass answers.
Piccolo and flutes play fast figures above the strings and the orchestra’s separated chords.
Long wind phrases sound above repeated muted-violin figures and plucked low strings.
Fast strings and woodwinds play against the returning brass call.
Winds and strings repeat short figures before the brass play again.
Upper winds and violins rush above brass chords and percussion.
The bell strikes D over quiet violin tremolo and pizzicato cellos.
Slow wind phrases sound above muted violins and sustained low strings.
The solo clarinet plays over divided violas and low strings; harp arpeggios follow its phrase.
The solo flute plays dolce above divided violas, cellos and plucked double basses.
Quiet wind chords and harp arpeggios settle on D major; the strings return for the last chord.

composer.epithet: Composer who could make a singer sound like a frightened child, a drunken monk or a tsar who could no longer bear his own thoughts.
facts: Piano with Anton Gerke; composition with Mily Balakirev, outside the conservatory
Guards officer until 1858; later a clerk in the Forestry Department and Government Control
Borodin, Cui, Balakirev, Rimsky-Korsakov; Vladimir Stasov and Viktor Hartmann
Boris Godunov, unfinished operas, three song cycles, Pictures at an Exhibition
composer.background:
When Borodin met Mussorgsky at a Saint Petersburg military hospital in 1856, the seventeen-year-old officer was immaculate, with a close-fitting uniform, polished manners and well-kept hands. He played extracts from Il trovatore and La traviata at the piano while admirers gathered round. Twenty-five years later, in another hospital, Repin painted the portrait that became his most familiar likeness. It shows a man in a dressing gown, his hair in disorder and his eyes still alert.

Mussorgsky was born at Karevo, on his family’s estate. His mother taught him the piano, and his nurse’s stories prompted the improvisations he remembered from childhood. At ten he was sent to school in Saint Petersburg, where he studied piano with Anton Gerke. He entered the School of Guards Cadets in 1852 and received a commission in the Preobrazhensky Regiment in 1856. His father paid for the publication of his first piano piece, a polka.
